The Administration's radical interpretation of Title VI is most apparent in its ``investigations'' into antisemitism at prominent colleges and research universities. These investigations were used as justification to cancel hundreds of millions of dollars in federal grants and contracts at Columbia University, Harvard University, Brown University, the University of California, Los Angeles, and other schools.\20\ Resembling less a standard civil rights investigation and more of a ``shakedown'', many schools reached agreements with the Administration, desperate to restore needed funding.\21\ In the instances where schools pushed back, we have seen courts recognize these institutions were compliant with Title VI, and should not have had their funding cut.\22\ Further, recent whistleblower allegations suggest that some of these investigations were based not on factual or legal analysis but political priorities, with punishments in some cases being determined before investigations were even completed.\23\

H.R. 9203 IGNORES THE ABANDONING OF DISPARATE IMPACT ANALYSIS TO FIGHT
RACIAL DISCRIMINATION
Data show that robust enforcement of compliance with Title VI's protections by programs receiving federal funds from the Department is necessary to achieve equity of educational opportunity.\24\ Remedies achieved through individual challenges under Title VI to discriminatory policies and practices were once an essential tool to bring about this robust enforcement, especially during periods of demonstrated hostility to proactive federal enforcement.\25\ Because racial discrimination is rarely explicit, identifying potential cases of discrimination by analyzing their impact--rather than just their motive--was critical to the enforcement of civil rights protections. Disparate impact theory was used for decades by private individuals in education settings, challenging practices that while facially race neutral, had an obvious disparate effect on Americans of different races or national origins.\26\ President Kennedy most eloquently explained the need for civil rights law to find violations linked to effect and not just to intent:
\24\U.S. Comm'n on Civil Rights, Are Rights a Reality? Evaluating Federal Civil Rights Enforcement 511, Nov. 2019, available at https:// www.usccr.gov/pubs/2019/11-21-Are-Rights-a- Reality.pdf.
\25\See Alexander v. Sandoval, 532U.S.275, 301-303(2001) (Stevens, J., dissenting).
\26\E.g. Lau v. Nichols, 414 U.S. 563 (1974).
``Simple justice requires that public funds, to which
all taxpayers of all races contribute, not be spent in
any fashion which encourages, entrenches, subsidizes,
or results in racial discrimination. Direct
discrimination by Federal, State, or local governments
is prohibited by the Constitution. But indirect
discrimination, through the use of Federal funds, is
just as invidious; and it should not be necessary to
resort to the courts to prevent each individual
violation.''\27\
\27\See H.R. Misc. Doc. No. 124, 88th Cong., 1st Sess. 3, 12
(1963).
In Alexander v. Sandoval,\28\ the Court overturned four decades of statutory protection against discrimination by removing the private right of action of individuals to bring cases based upon disparate impact, leaving federal agencies as the only entities that can enforce disparate impact regulations. Since 2001, private citizens may have their civil rights violated under Title VI in a way that can only be proven via a disparate impact test, but if the government is not willing to take administrative action on their behalf, they have no remedy.
\28\532 U.S. 275 (2001).
On April 25, 2025, President Trump issued Executive Order 14281, denouncing disparate impact theory and directing the Attorney General ``to initiate appropriate action to repeal or amend the implementing regulations for Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 for all agencies to the extent they contemplate disparate-impact liability.''\29\ The Department of Education rescinded its Title VI regulations via a Final rule on July 24, 2026 without warning or opportunity for public comment.\30\ Following its regulatory retreat, the Department has also rescinded guidance related to school discipline--an area where studies have consistently found that Black and Brown students are disproportionately subject to exclusionary discipline (suspensions and exclusions) than similarly situated White students.\31\
\29\Exec. Order No. 14281, 90 Fed. Reg. 17537 (Apr. 28, 2025) (``It is the policy of the United States to eliminate the use of disparate-impact liability in all contexts to the maximum degree possible to avoid violating the Constitution, Federal civil rights laws, and basic American ideals.'').
\30\Rescinding Portions of the Department of Education Title VI Regulations To Align With the Statutory Text and Conform to Executive Order 14281, 90 Fed. Reg. 46733 (July 23, 2026).
\31\Press Release, U.S. Department of Education Directs Schools to Stop Racial Balancing in Student Discipline Policies, Investigates Two School Districts, Aug. 18, 2026, https://www.ed. gov/about/news/press-release/us-department-of-education-directs-schools-stop-racial-balancing-student-discipline-policies-investigates-two-school-districts; See Cory Turner, When Is Suspending Students Discrimination? Education Department Renews An Old Fight, Nat'l Pub. Radio, Aug. 25, 2025, https://www.npr.org/2026/08/25/nx-s1-5936474/discrimination-school-discipline-suspension-race-education-department-civil-rights, (``Multiple federal investigations have found that discrimination still plagues America's schools, even as it's been illegal for decades, thanks to federal civil rights law . . . . In late 2018, OCR reachedan agreement with Wake County Public School System in North Carolina after finding that, among other things, Black students being disciplined for their first offense were more likely to be suspended than similarly situated white students.'').
These are some, but not all of the actions taken by the Trump Administration that strongly suggest they are either unwilling or unable to enforce Title VI in a fair and equitable manner. They continue to try and turn Title VI on its head in an effort to turn the clock back on civil rights.
SUMMARY OF CONCERNS ON H.R. 9203
While it is not a fatal flaw, we are perplexed that H.R. 9203 places new requirements on compliance with Title VI, without amending Title VI itself. The decision to place requirements and penalties related to Title VI compliance in HEA was likely made to avoid amendment of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Such amendment would likely implicate the jurisdiction of the Committee on the Judiciary. But this is something the Committee has considered in the past and successfully overcome.
In 2019, then-Chairman Bobby Scott (D-VA) first introduced the Equity and Inclusion Enforcement Act (EIEA) in the 116th Congress.\32\ In addition to restoring the private right of action for disparate impact liability, the bill requires all recipients of federal funds under Title VI (K-12 schools and IHEs) to have Title VI Monitors, nearly identical to those required under Title IX, and similar to what is required under H.R. 9203. Unlike H.R. 9203, EIEA includes provisions that amend the Civil Rights Act of 1964--squarely in the jurisdiction of the Committee on the Judiciary--and provisions related to requirements of staffing at the Department of Education, squarely in the Committee on Education and Workforce's jurisdiction. In 2019, as the bill had been referred to both Committees, after our Committee marked the bill up, we were able to reach an agreement with the Judiciary Committee regarding a discharge of their consideration and the bill went to the floor and was passed.\33\ The Majority in this instance could have done the same thing with H.R. 9203 but chose not to. By choosing to limit the operative clauses to the HEA, the compliance provisions of H.R. 9203 do not apply to all educational settings receiving federal assistance, but just colleges and universities that participate in the Federal Student Aid program. K-12 schools and IHEs that do not participate in federal student aid, are not bound by H.R. 9203's requirements. The Majority should work with its counterparts on the Committee on the Judiciary to settle any lingering issues so that the scope of H.R. 9203 eventually mirrors that of Title VI itself, that is, all educational programs receiving federal assistance.
